rewrite.hint: x is a fresh object literal assigned straight to T. Ask how TypeScript treats a property the target type never declares.
rewrite.explanation: Pick<{ a: 1; b: 2 }, "a"> is { a: 1 }, and a fresh object literal is checked for excess properties, so tsc reports "Object literal may only specify known properties, and 'b' does not exist in type 'T'". The property is not dropped: the emitted JavaScript still carries b, and nothing is checked at runtime. Assigning the same value through a variable is accepted, which is exactly why the literal check exists - it catches typos and stale fields where you write them.

rationale: Verified, and excess-property checking on fresh literals is one of the highest-value rules in this part of the topic because it catches misspelled and stale fields. Only the option shapes, hint and explanation depth need work.

rewrite.hint: Work out the exact type Omit produces first, then check whether { b: 5 } supplies everything that type requires.
rewrite.explanation: Omit<{ a: number; b: number }, "a"> is { b: number }, so { b: 5 } provides every property the type declares and the assignment is accepted. a is not missing: it is not part of T at all, which is the difference from Partial, where a would still be allowed but optional. Nothing is checked at runtime, because the annotation is erased before the code runs.

rationale: Verified, and it pairs usefully with rm-ts-147: the derived type is what a value is checked against, once from the failing side and once from the passing side. Options, hint and explanation need the local fixes.
evidence: tsc: type T = Omit<{ a: number; b: number }, "a">; const x: T = { b: 5 } -> no errors, exit status 0 (TypeScript 5.9.3, --strict)

rewrite.hint: Every key is listed for removal. Ask what is left of an object type when no properties remain, and whether that is the same as no type at all.
rewrite.explanation: Omit is Pick<T, Exclude<keyof T, K>>, and excluding both keys leaves no keys, so T is {} - an object type that declares nothing. never is the empty type that no value has; {} is close to the opposite, since almost any value satisfies it. tsc accepts both const y: T = { z: 1 } and const n: T = 5 for this T, which is why an accidental Omit<T, keyof T> in generic code quietly stops checking anything.

rationale: Verified edge case with a genuinely instructive distractor (never), let down by malformed option syntax and an explanation that never contrasts the two. The csDrift flag is only the translated parenthetical after {}.
